Every model so far predicted a *number*; this week the outcome is yes or no (arrest or not, reoffend or desist), which is the form most criminal-justice questions actually take. A straight line can't live on a 0/1 outcome, so probability becomes odds, then log-odds, and `lm()` becomes `glm(family = binomial)`. It's also the week we return to the Session 1 bank-robbery model you couldn't read: re-fit and finally read, line by line. This is the last session of new statistical content: the toolbox is complete, and Checkpoint 4 (the final one) fits your actual project model.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this week you can:

- explain why `lm()` fails on a 0/1 outcome, and how moving from probability to odds to log-odds fixes it
- fit a logistic regression with `glm(family = binomial)` and read its output
- translate coefficients into odds ratios *and* predicted probabilities, and keep the two straight
- say logistic results in plain language a police chief could act on, without confusing odds with probability

## Before class

- Read: Stanton **Ch. 10** (Logistic Regression)
- No new packages. If you want to spin the 3D surface on your own machine, `install.packages("plotly")` is optional.

## In class

- Why criminal justice runs on binary outcomes (arrest, failure to appear, re-arrest, intoxicated or not), and why `lm()` predicts impossible probabilities when you feed it one
- **Closing the loop on Session 1:** the bank-robbery case study that opened the course was a logistic regression: we re-fit the exact model and finally read its table (coefficients are log-odds; `exp()` them into odds ratios; West Zone's odds ratio is why the cars went west)
- Probability → odds → log-odds, and why a straight line can only live on the last of the three
- `glm(family = binomial)`, one argument away from `lm()`, and the two interpretation moves: **odds ratios** for effects, **predicted probabilities** for cases
- **The 3D logistic surface:** Session 10's flat plane, bent into an S-shaped probability sheet
- Real-data thread: which Chicago community areas are **high violence**? Unemployment (OR ≈ 1.45 per point) and vacant housing (OR ≈ 1.33 per point) both raise the odds; predicted probabilities run from ~3% (Forest Glen) to over 99% (West Garfield Park). Associations, not causes, and we say so.
- **Lab 11:** the whole workflow yourself: Chicago walkthrough, then your own model of injury crashes in the Alaska data (does an intoxicated driver raise the odds that anyone is hurt, holding driver age and the number of vehicles constant?), plus odds-ratio translation drills
